lines.text: hear Him here we shall hear Him nowhere. To be sure, God
is present in nature. But Luther's dictum remains true: "If
God's word and sign is not there and is not recognized, then
it avails nothing even though God Himself were there!" No,
nature is not the sphere of God's self-revelation. Nevertheless,
Scripture declares that God is effectually present in nature.
"The heavens are telling the glory of God and the firmament
proclaims His handiwork. Day to day pours forth speech,
and night to night declares knowledge. There is no speech
nor are there words; their voice is not heard" (Ps. I9: 2-4).
He, the Omnipotent and Omnipresent, is also present in
nature. We to whom He speaks in the word of Scripture and
the gospel of Jesus Christ are not intended to come to know
Him first from the world of nature. But as those who already
know Him through Jesus Christ, we are intended to look for
the witness to His presence which is implicit in nature, and
to praise and worship Him with grateful hearts for the traces
of His being which we see there. Hence we do not speak
of God's self-disclosure in nature but we do speak of God's
presence in nature. The question is: in what way do we
encounter this presence?
It is unquestionable that the glad and grateful appreciation
of the beauty and vitality of nature is not peculiar to
Christians, but is characteristic of all men who are not
inwardly consumed by care and grief. It is unquestionable
too that this joy in nature is not a merely aesthetic attitude.
Such joy is essentially different from the joy we feel in the
contemplation of a beautiful picture or a great work of art.
Nature does not invite us to merely recreative or cultural
attitudes. The feeling with which we walk through the
fields and woods in spring and delight in their deepening
green, or with which the town-dweller cultivates his little
garden plot and rejoices to see its growth, is a feeling which
has a quite characteristic tone. It is a joy in which the whole
